text:
Synthesized Practice Interview
(Interviewer:) Thanks for sitting down with me. I'd love to hear about a big decision you've made recently – something that's been on your mind.
(Participant:) Yeah, sure. So I quit my job about three months ago. It was a good job, stable, benefits, the whole thing. People thought I was crazy.
(Interviewer:) Tell me more about what was going on before you made that decision.
(Participant:) I'd been there six years. And for the last two, I kept having this feeling on Sunday nights – like this dread. Not about Monday specifically, just about the pattern. I'd think, "Is this really what the next thirty years looks like?" And that question scared me more than quitting did.
(Interviewer:) That Sunday night feeling – can you walk me through what that was actually like?
(Participant:) It's hard to describe. It wasn't panic. It was more like... [pause] heaviness. I'd be doing dishes or something normal and I'd just feel flat. And I have this rule with myself – if something makes me feel flat for more than a few months, it's not a phase, it's a signal. I kept ignoring it because the job checked every box on paper.
(Interviewer:) So what finally tipped it?
(Participant:) Honestly? A conversation with my dad. He retired last year, and he said something like, "I spent so long being responsible that I forgot what I actually liked." And I just sat there in his kitchen thinking, "That's going to be me." I gave my notice two weeks later. [laugh] My mom was less enthusiastic.
(Interviewer:) How did you feel right after you told your manager?
(Participant:) Terrified. And then weirdly relieved, like when you finally say the thing you've been rehearsing in the shower for months. My hands were shaking, but I also felt lighter than I had in a really long time. I went home and just sat on my couch and thought, "Okay. Now what?" But it was the good kind of "now what."
(Interviewer:) And where are you now with it? Three months in?
(Participant:) Some days are great. Some days I wake up at 3 a.m. doing math in my head about savings. But I keep telling myself – the discomfort of not knowing is different from the discomfort of knowing you're in the wrong place. I'd rather have the first one.

text:
Synthesized Practice Interview
(Interviewer:) I appreciate you being here. I'd like to talk about something significant that's happened in your family recently, if you're open to it.
(Participant:) Sure. The big thing is my mom. We moved her into assisted living about two months ago.
(Interviewer:) How did that come about?
(Participant:) It was a long time coming. She'd been living alone since my dad passed, and at first she was fine. Independent, sharp. But over the last year, little things started adding up. She'd leave the stove on. She called me once at midnight confused about what day it was. And I kept thinking, "It's just a bad week," but the bad weeks stopped ending.
(Interviewer:) When you say you kept thinking it was a bad week – what was going on inside your head during that time?
(Participant:) I was bargaining with myself. Like, "If she can manage the grocery trip on her own, she's okay." I kept setting these little tests in my mind, and she kept barely passing them, which let me tell myself it wasn't time yet. [pause] I think I needed it to not be time yet.
(Interviewer:) Tell me about the moment when that shifted.
(Participant:) She fell in the bathroom. Nothing broken, thank god, but she was on the floor for a couple hours before she called me. And when I got there, she was embarrassed more than hurt. She said, "Don't you dare make a big deal out of this." And I didn't, in front of her. But I sat in my car in her driveway afterward and just cried. Because I knew.
(Interviewer:) How has the transition been for the two of you?
(Participant:) She hates it. [small laugh] She's polite about it, but I can tell. She keeps rearranging the furniture like she's trying to make it hers. For me, there's this weird mix of guilt and relief. I feel guilty for the relief, which is its own fun cycle. But I sleep better knowing someone's there if she falls again.
(Interviewer:) You mentioned guilt. Can you tell me what that sounds like in your head?
(Participant:) It's my mom's voice, honestly. [laugh] She raised us to handle things ourselves. So there's this part of me that says, "You should have moved her in with you. That's what family does." But I have a rule now – I don't let guilt make my decisions anymore. Guilt is a feeling, not a plan. The plan has to work for everyone, not just the person who feels bad.

text:
Synthesized Practice Interview
(Interviewer:) Thanks for coming in. I'd love to hear about something you've been working toward recently – a goal, a project, anything like that.
(Participant:) I ran a half marathon last month. Which is insane to me, because two years ago I couldn't run a mile without wanting to die. [both laugh]
(Interviewer:) So take me back. What got you started?
(Participant:) My doctor, bluntly. She told me my blood pressure was heading somewhere bad and basically said, "You're 38. Fix this now or manage it forever." And I remember driving home from that appointment thinking, "I don't want to be the person who manages it. I want to be the person who fixed it."
(Interviewer:) That distinction seems important to you – managing versus fixing.
(Participant:) Huge. Because managing felt like accepting defeat. Like, "Okay, this is who I am now, pass the pills." And fixing felt like... I don't know, agency? Like I still had a say. So I started walking. Then jogging. Then I found a running group, which honestly saved me because I would've quit alone.
(Interviewer:) Tell me about the running group. What was that like?
(Participant:) Terrifying at first. I was the slowest by a lot. And I have this thing where I hate being the worst at something in public. Like, I will avoid it entirely rather than be bad in front of people. But I kept showing up because I told myself, "The embarrassment lasts an hour. The regret of quitting lasts way longer." That became my little mantra. [laugh]
(Interviewer:) What was crossing the finish line like?
(Participant:) I cried. Like, full ugly cry. [laugh] My wife was there with a sign, and I just lost it. Not because it was fast or impressive – my time was terrible – but because I genuinely didn't think I was that person. I had this identity of myself as someone who wasn't athletic. And crossing that line broke it. That identity just... cracked open.
(Interviewer:) Has that changed how you think about yourself beyond running?
(Participant:) Yeah, actually. I catch myself now when I say "I'm not a ____ person." Because I said that about running for 38 years and it turned out to be completely wrong. So now when I hear myself say "I'm not a morning person" or "I'm not good at that," I think, "Is that true, or is that just the story I've been telling?"
